paragraphs.text: OpenAI wants to stop calling its AI facilities data centers and start calling them AI compute campuses, according to reports from Axios, TechCrunch and Business Insider on November 1, 2026. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the term to Business Insider that day.

The spokesperson told Business Insider that the new name better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure the company is building for AI. The company described the sites as long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work, and said it wants host communities to help shape them and share in the opportunities they create.

The rebrand is one piece of a wider public relations push that OpenAI is preparing for after the United States midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, Axios reported, as summarized by TechCrunch. Democrats appear likely to win back the House and possibly the Senate, according to TechCrunch, and Axios reported that OpenAI was preparing for a possible blue wave that could bring a more regulation-minded government.
Other ideas in the plan include developing AI speed limits, showing people how AI helps them in daily life and pushing the United States to help shape global AI standards, TechCrunch reported.
Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, told Axios that the midterms will be a preview of the 2028 presidential race, where he expects AI to be a central issue, according to TechCrunch.
Why data centers became a campaign issue

Data centers have become a major issue for voters in this election cycle, Business Insider reported. It cited a recent Pew Research poll in which 54% of Americans said AI data centers are bad for the environment.

Other large technology companies have tried to win over local communities with money. Meta, Amazon and Microsoft have pledged millions of dollars to communities and schools near their data centers, according to Business Insider.

Lehane called the debate over data centers good and healthy, TechCrunch reported. The outlet noted that the debate has already led Amazon and Microsoft to say they will stop using nondisclosure agreements in negotiations with local governments. Lehane also said communities should hold companies accountable so they receive a real benefit from the projects.
Business Insider noted that it is unclear whether the compute campus name will catch on.

A new name does not change what these sites need: land, power, water and local approval. The term campus suggests jobs and long-term presence rather than a sealed warehouse of servers, which is the image opponents tend to use. How far the label travels will likely depend less on OpenAI's messaging than on whether towns that host these projects see concrete benefits, such as tax revenue, local hiring and fair power prices. The pairing of the rebrand with talk of AI speed limits also shows OpenAI preparing for a Washington that may be more skeptical of the industry after the vote.
Watch whether OpenAI's partners and local officials start using the compute campus label in permit filings and project announcements after the November 3 midterms.
